newsitem.title: JAPAN: Gore in Japan on trip to boost U.S.-Sino ties.
newsitem.headline: Gore in Japan on trip to boost U.S.-Sino ties.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore arrived in Japan on Sunday for consultations before going on to China for talks he said were designed to build on signs of improving U.S.-China relations.
"This visit is intended to reaffirm once again America's commitment to the region overall," Gore said during an arrival ceremony held in steady rain.
"The security and prosperity of the United States is vitally tied to the Asia-Pacific region," said the vice president.

Gore, whose eight-day trip to Asia includes a stop in South Korea, was to meet Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Monday before heading to Beijing that night for talks on Tuesday with Chinese President Jiang Zemin.

Chatting with reporters on board Air Force Two, Gore sounded upbeat about the chances for improving relations with China -- a nation Washington frequently has clashed with in recent years, particularly over trade, Taiwan and human rights.
"Change is taking place rapidly inside China ... the growth of the free sector of their economy is far outstripping the growth in the state-owned sector," he said.

"Both our countries are clearly signalling to one another that we want to find a way to move forward in the relationship," said Gore, who planned to discuss a broad range of issues that included the environment and the future of Hong Kong.
"I hope to have meaningful discussions in China," said Gore, adding that he would "touch on every issue that has a particular impact for our two countries".
Gore will be the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit Beijing since troops brutally ended pro-democracy demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in 1989.

At least part of his discussions will deal with preparations for an exchange of visits by U.S. President Bill Clinton and Jiang. The Chinese leader is expected to visit the United States late this year and Clinton tentatively plans to go to China in 1998.

Gore said that high on his agenda was a discussion about possible four-way talks between the two Koreas and the United States and China, an idea that was proposed in April by Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam.
The four-way talks would be designed to bring a formal end to the Korea War, something Washington hopes would serve as a way to defuse tensions on the Korean Peninsula permanently.
Gore's bid for improved relations between Washington and Beijing comes as conservatives in the U.S. Congress have been developing a get-tough attitude towards the Chinese government.
Gore said that before he left Washington he spoke several times with Newt Gingrich, the Republican speaker of the House of Representatives, who is heading a fact-finding mission to the region.
"We discussed the goals for the trip ... we want to make sure that we get what is in the best interests of the United States of America," Gore said.
